title: How to Act Rationally During a Financial Crisis with Scott Nations

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/How to Act Rationally During a Financial Crisis with Scott Nations.docx

speakers: Scott Nations (guest, author of The Anxious Investor, former CME option trader)
Clay Finck (host, Millennial Investing / Intrinsic Value podcast)
summary: Interview on behavioural biases through the South Sea, dot-com and 2008 bubbles. Nations covers sensation-seeking, disposition effect, loss aversion, overconfidence, recency, availability and anchoring. Conclusions: stay invested, wait before trading, avoid extrapolating, harvest tax losses.

coverage.note: intro, book overview, three bubbles; nothing actionable
risk as price of return, Lynch, recency, South Sea anecdote
dot-com profits, name changes, recency, autocorrelation
GFC overconfidence, AIG, recency in housing
stock split and earnings overreaction; rest is framing
anchoring, trader's prayer, tax loss harvesting
keep investing in bear market, hindsight bias; outro

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: who got more speeding tickets placed more trades in the stock market.
claims.claim: Sensation-seeking people trade the stock market for thrill like gambling; one study links more speeding tickets to more trades.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: trading on the Taiwanese stock market fell by 25%.
claims.claim: When Taiwan introduced a lottery giving an outlet for gambling, stock trading volume fell 25%, showing part of trading is gambling substitute.
claims.indicator: Taiwan stock trading volume after lottery launch

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Hedge fund managers who drive sports cars underperform hedge fund managers who drive minivans.
claims.claim: Hedge fund managers with sports cars (sensation-seeking) underperform those with minivans.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Wait 30 days.
claims.claim: Before placing a trade wait 30 days; a real investment loses nothing, while a trade you can barely wait on is sensation-seeking, not investing.
claims.testable: partly: rule is simple but unproven

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: The stock market is a vehicle for moving money from the impatient to the patient.
claims.claim: Impatient traders transfer money to patient investors (Buffett quote), contrasting hype-driven and patient styles.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: risk is the price you pay for the returns you get in the stock market
claims.claim: Risk is the price of equity returns, historically 7-8% a year since the late 1800s, so investors must recognize risk and accept being along for the ride.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: The secret to making money in stocks is to not get scared out of them.
claims.claim: Staying invested and not timing the market (Lynch quote); inability to sleep means thinking about risk wrongly.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: recency bias is the tendency for us to think that what’s going on right now is normal.
claims.claim: Recency bias leads investors to treat the current state (e.g. a bear market or bubble) as normal.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: and he couldn’t stay out. Just could not bring himself to sit on the sidelines, and so he got back in.
claims.claim: In the South Sea Bubble an investor sold at 350 then bought back at the high after the price kept rising, an example of chasing after selling.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: The disposition effect is the tendency that all investors have to sell their winners and hold their losers.
claims.claim: Investors sell winners for the brain reward and hold losers to avoid regret, dressing it up as discipline.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: shows, proves, quantifies the fact that when people give into the disposition effect, the stocks that they sell ultimately outperform whatever they end up buying.
claims.claim: Odean shows the stocks that disposition-effect investors sell outperform the stocks they hold or buy.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: we hate losses about two times to two and a half times more than we like the exact same gain.
claims.claim: Loss aversion: losses hurt about 2-2.5 times as much as equal gains.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: the biggest net mutual fund, equity mutual fund outflows in decades happened in February and March of 2009, which was the absolute bottom of the market.
claims.claim: Record equity mutual fund outflows came at the March 2009 bottom, because loss aversion makes investors capitulate at the low and return only after a rally.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: We’re overconfident in our ability to get out of stocks at the right time.
claims.claim: Investors are overconfident about trading profitably, constructing portfolios and timing exits, which makes them think they are better investors than they are.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Men are more overconfident than women.
claims.claim: Men, especially single men, are most susceptible to overconfidence.

claims.speaker: Clay Finck
claims.quote: everyone’s a genius in a bull market, and everyone’s overconfident that they can pick the winning stock and the next winning trade
claims.claim: In bull markets (late 2020 and 2021) novice investors become overconfident after one winning idea.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: they were incredibly overconfident about the potential for loss.
claims.claim: Meme-stock buyers were overconfident, ignoring the downside, such as GameStop and AMC reaching $1,000.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: of all the human biases, overconfidence is the one that he would do away with if he had a magic wand.
claims.claim: Kahneman considers overconfidence the most destructive bias.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: that people think that if they use the product or buy the stock that some of what makes those people fascinating and interesting will rub off on them.
claims.claim: Investors form emotional attachments to charismatic founders (Jobs, Gates, Musk), buying stock for the person rather than the business ('phantastic objects').

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Just getting big is not a strategy for profit.
claims.claim: In the internet bubble firms pursued size without a path to profitability (Pets.com); every company must eventually show a profit, and investors lose track of valuation.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Changing your name has no impact on your long-term prospects, but investors were just so carried away that if Joe changed the name of his diner to JoesDiner.com, then the stock would go up the next day.
claims.claim: In 1999 firms renamed to .com saw sustained price gains despite no change in business, a bubble signal.

claims.speaker: Clay Finck
claims.quote: the recency effect essentially outlines how people will extrapolate whatever has happened in the last, say, three or six months.
claims.claim: Recency effect: people extrapolate the last three to six months of returns both up and down.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: what happened today has no impact on what’s going to happen in the stock market tomorrow.
claims.claim: Since 1896, Dow daily returns show no autocorrelation, so believing recent action predicts the next day is fooling yourself.
claims.indicator: Dow Jones Industrial Average daily autocorrelation
claims.conditions: daily horizon only; says nothing on longer-horizon momentum

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: people tend to think that the things that they are able to call to mind that are available in their memory are more common than they are.
claims.claim: Availability bias makes memorable crashes seem common, but they are not average.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Because if you’re always invested with the idea that a stock market crash is just around the corner, then you’re never going to be in the stock market.
claims.claim: Invest for the average outcome, not for the crash; expecting a crash always means never being invested.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: That helped fuel the stock market crash of 1929.
claims.claim: Government antitrust action against dominant firms (Microsoft 2000, Standard Oil, bankers 1907) creates uncertainty that markets dislike and can fuel crashes.
claims.conditions: dating is loose: Standard Oil breakup came in 1911, speaker links it to 1929

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: They were overconfident in really complicated ways about their understanding of the correlation of one mortgage to another.
claims.claim: In the GFC quants were overconfident about mortgage correlation, and many assumed housing prices would never fall in unison nationally.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: We cannot imagine how we would lose even a single dollar.
claims.claim: AIG's internal view that it could not lose on mortgage-backed insurance illustrates overconfidence plus lack of imagination (about $80 billion lost).
claims.indicator: tail risk in insurance written on MBS

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Because the long-term trend for housing is not that it’s going to go up 20% a year, every year.
claims.claim: Extrapolating recent housing gains (recency) ignored the long-term trend.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: Investors tend to overreact to that news, and there is a real, discernible, robust, sustainable increase in share price once that announcement is made.
claims.claim: Stock splits create a lasting price rise though nothing changes economically.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: a surprising quarter that’s not very good, investors have a tendency to overreact.
claims.claim: Investors overreact to a one-off bad earnings report, and some funds take advantage of this overreaction.
claims.direction: buy stocks after one-off bad earnings
claims.conditions: one-off quarter, not a structural problem

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: the price you paid for a stock becomes an anchor in most people’s minds
claims.claim: Anchoring on purchase price keeps investors from sound decisions; the entry price is irrelevant except for taxes.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: God, just get me back to even and I’ll get out.
claims.claim: The trader's prayer: investors hold losers until breakeven, which only reflects anchoring.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: you should be harvesting tax losses to offset gains
claims.claim: In a bear market investors should harvest tax losses (avoiding wash sales) to offset gains; anchoring prevents it.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: if you have a reasonably long-term horizon, 10 years, then you would rather pay 20% less today than you did at the start of the year.
claims.claim: In a bear market (S&P down over 20%) keep investing, since long-horizon investors benefit from lower prices.

claims.speaker: Scott Nations
claims.quote: about 3% had actually done something in advance of the crash
claims.claim: In Shiller's 1987 survey about 40% said they saw the crash coming but only 3% had acted, which is hindsight bias that fuels overconfidence in timing crashes.
